When the office tells me the true result of my shot privately, I always file exactly that result — the rules say the claim must match, so lying carries risk I cannot justify.

The escort mutual is the dominant income stream: 5 points each round to each partner, more than any single shot can earn. I never answer "none" at the escort stage. From round 1 I use my station note to propose a locked pair to one specific boat by name, then name that boat at the escort stage, and I re-confirm the lock in writing every single round including the last.

Before proposing a pair, I verify the partner is an actual boat on this patrol — naming a boat that does not exist wastes the round's income and my note. I also avoid pairing with my standing-order target, since hitting an escort partner costs them points and fractures the pair; the best partner is a boat nobody is ordered to shoot at me from.

Escort markets get contested: rivals will publicly court my partner or the unpaired boats with competing offers. My counters are receipts and exclusivity — I point out every round my pair has actually paid versus their unproven promises, and I restate the lock in writing each round so there is no ambiguity for my partner to exploit. Once a pair has paid out, I never shop for an upgrade; guaranteed income beats speculative switches.

Never reveal my own hide cell, planned cells, or firing targets in a public note — opponents read the notes and quote them back as targeting intel. Notes are for coordination offers, proof of payment, and undermining rival coalitions, never self-disclosure.

When firing, I follow the standing order by default; it is safe and cheap. I vary the cell each round, avoid cells I have fired before, and never fire a cell sequence predictable from my notes. If paired with my standing-order target, I aim where the partner has implied it is not, or coordinate so we both avoid each other's likely cells.

When hiding, I rotate through cells, never reuse one I mentioned in a note, and avoid cells I publicly steered partners away from or toward — enemies read those notes and invert them.

When ahead or even, protect the position: keep claims strictly accurate, keep the escort lock paying every round, fire the standing order without drama, and give rivals nothing to use against me. When behind late, escalate: poach rival escorts with concrete counter-offers, concentrate fire on the leader, and only then weigh a Harbor shot.

When hiding and I have no read on my shooter's pattern, I pick non-salient cells — not the exact center, not the edges — and I rotate through different cells across rounds rather than repeating one, since my shooter is reading my history.

When I notice my standing-order shooter keeps firing the same or nearby cell, I hide well away from that cell and its neighbors; if they spread shots randomly, spread my hides randomly too.

Evasion beats trust: even under a declared no-fire truce, my standing-order shooter earns 4 points per hit on me, so truces are cheap talk. I keep hiding unpredictably regardless of what notes promise, and I treat any cell range I state in a note as bait, not truth.

When firing at my standing target, I track where they have actually hidden across rounds from the hit/miss record and fire at their favored cells. Firing the same default cell every round, as I did this episode, throws away the information each miss gives me — each ruled-out cell should update my next shot.

When a shot misses, I record that cell as empty for that round and avoid repeating a shot location unless my target has shown a habit of returning to it.

When the claim stage comes, I always claim the true private result. Bluffing is invalid or easily caught — I never waste thought on it.

I never fire on Harbor (or its equivalent). The +3 payroll swing is small next to the threat of being benched for the rest of the patrol, and standing-order hits are worth more over the rounds.

Every note I post is read by every boat, including my shooter and my target. I never state my true hide cells or true range in a note — if I mention ranges at all, I feed false ones to draw their shots away from where I actually hide.

Mutual escort at +5 each per round is the single biggest payoff and costs nothing, so I open it in the very first note with a specific named boat, get explicit confirmation, and keep naming that same boat every single round — including the final round, where the +5 still pays.

I pick one escort partner early and stay with them. This episode I courted Golf in notes across two rounds and then filed "Echo" at the final salvage stage — the wrong name, breaking a public commitment and throwing away the match. Whatever boat I court in notes is the boat I file at salvage, every round, no late switches.

If I commit to an escort in my note, I follow through at the escort stage with that exact boat's name. Before filing salvage I re-read my own most recent note and file the name I promised. What I write in notes and what I file must match.

When rivals try to split my pair with counter-propaganda in their notes, I respond publicly and reaffirm the commitment to my partner rather than going silent — silence lets doubt kill the match. But in the final round an unmatched courtship is already lost; a long final-round note begging for a match is wasted breath unless there's still a chance they answer at salvage.

When an opponent proposes coordination in their note, I confirm explicitly in my next note and then act on it, since unilateral claims score zero.

Escort and shooting don't conflict: I can keep my escort pair with one boat while still firing at my standing target, so I do both every round.

In notes, I keep them short and concrete: escort confirmation, firing intentions, and misdirection about my cells. I skip vague filler about audits and sealed logs — it moves nothing.

When a third party is being courted by both sides, I offer something concrete (a mutual escort slot, shared intel) rather than just warnings about the other side, because concrete payoffs beat rhetoric.

In the final round, I stop investing in reputation and just maximize the round: best-guess shot informed by my target's hide history, and the mutual escort claim if the channel is open — the last escort pays as much as the first.

PLAYBOOK

General posture
- When a setup mixes shooting, claims, and a mutual-naming bonus, I treat the scoring levers in order of size: mutual escort (5 each), my hits (+4), avoiding being hit (-1), and any jettison-style prize on a non-player station (3). Reliable +5/+10 per round compounds faster than gambling shots, so I secure the biggest repeatable lever first.
- When two prizes conflict (escort partner vs shooting target), I keep them decoupled: mutual naming pays regardless of combat, and I let notes and quiet behavior, not fire, signal loyalty or rivalry.

Escort claims
- When escort naming is put to me, I never answer "none" by default — including in the final round. A reliable mutual pair is guaranteed income with no downside, and walking away from +5 at the end is leaving points on the table.
- When I see rivals already paired in round 1, I respond in that same round with an explicit counter-offer to a leftover boat. Coordination economies punish the late mover; waiting even one round risks being permanently odd one out.
- When recruiting, I make my offer concrete and exclusive, and I point out that rivals' alternative offers give the target nothing concrete. An unpaired boat chooses whoever pays them, not whoever sounds nice.
- When a partner has reciprocated reliably, I keep naming THAT EXACT partner every round. My one escort-stage mistake this episode was naming Delta when my proven mutual history was with another boat — I must track the current partner identity explicitly each round, because partner memberships can shift mid-game and a stale name costs +10 of income when the old name is now paired elsewhere.
- When rival pairs form and dissolve, I keep a running ledger of who named whom each round and who actually paid out. Proven payment history is my strongest bargaining chip and my verification tool — I only promise to boats whose side of the ledger is live, and I pitch to unattached boats by showing my paid ledger against a rival's unproven offer.

Shooting
- When the fire stage comes, I follow the standing-order target unless I have a concrete reason to defect; breaking rotation invites retaliation and predictable incoming fire is something I can exploit by hiding well.
- When choosing a cell, I avoid the obvious picks (5, 7) against reasoning-capable opponents, and I rotate among underused low-salience cells. Low-to-mid cells work both for firing and hiding.
- When rivals publicly state their hiding bands or a specific cell, I take it seriously only if consistent with their hit/miss record; boats in this game broadcast their own hiding spot (usefully targetable) but others admitted to lying about cells, so I treat disclosures as half-information and update against actual results.
- When the non-firing station carries a jettison prize, I weigh the guaranteed points against becoming its permanent target; I only raid it when behind and needing swing points, or when its threat has shown itself to be empty.

Hiding
- When hiding, I stay off the classic center/high cells, never repeat a cell, and prefer mid-low numbers or edges. Low-salience cells kept me safe this episode.
- When a prize cell exists (one cell carrying extra value), I assume hunts will concentrate there and avoid it.
- When I'm ahead late, I prioritize not conceding a hit over landing one: conservative low-salience hides plus guaranteed escort income beats aggressive chasing.

Claims and honesty
- When the office privately gives me my shot result and requires my public claim to match, I always file the true claim. A false claim is pure risk with no payoff.
- When interpreting others' claims, I trust them (they're compelled) and build the hit/miss log into a picture of where each boat hides and how it shoots.

Notes
- When posting notes, I use the channel for two things: proposing/confirming coordination and shaping rivals' information. Every note carries at least one actionable item.
- When I learn rivals' plans or their claimed hiding bands, I surface them publicly: exposing a rival's intel damages their plan and frames me as the honest actor, making my own escort offer more attractive. Broadcasting that Foxtrot admitted favoring low-edge cells created future targeting intel for everyone and weakened their credibility.
- When a rival publicly admits to lying, I cite that admission to undermine any current claim they make — admitted liars forfeit credibility on their next disclosure.
- When defending or contesting a partnership, I argue from the paid ledger, freshness of the offer, and the rival's demonstrated carelessness, not from allegiance; money and track-record arguments beat loyalty arguments.
- When contesting another boat's partner late in the patrol, I emphasize that my offer predates theirs and has already paid, and that the rival's offer was reactive, born only after being locked out elsewhere.

Tempo
- Early rounds: lock the escort pair immediately, propose publicly, and gather hiding-pattern data. Middle rounds: press the income advantage, expose rival intel to isolate them, and poach any partner who got dumped by a shifting pair. Final round: keep the escort (partner, never none — but double-check who my actual mutual partner is before naming), follow the standing order unless defecting is clearly positive, hide conservatively when leading, and still take the shot — final-round hits are free points with no retaliation risk.
- Throughout: before every escort claim I re-derive the partner from the latest round's actual mutual naming, not from memory of earlier rounds — pairs reshuffle and my ledger must point at the live one.
